With the starting model, 70% of the candidate programs run but only 34% pass verification, so about half of the programs that run draw the wrong content, and 48.9% of specifications receive a verified program. After one round the share is 95.2%, and it stays between 95% and 97% in later rounds, including the round that switches to new topics. Horizontal bars rise from 11.8% to 98.4%, and scatter plots from 23.4% to 90.9% (Appendix E ). Sampling the writer’s correct programs on weak values more often does not explain this gain. When we retrain the first-round understanding update with these programs drawn uniformly and every other example unchanged, the resulting writer passes verification on the same 5,376 second-round specifications at the same rate as ours (90.8% for both). As a side effect, writing the programs of a round takes 18 rather than 159 GPU hours, so each new round of data is much faster to build. Reading program renders. Correct renders test whether the reader confirms requirements that the image meets. Held-out edited renders come from first-round specifications that no round trains on, so every reader is measured on the same images. On questions whose answer the edit changes, a reader that answers from the request instead of the image is wrong. On correct renders, accuracy rises from 87.1% to 99.3% after four rounds, and binding rises from 77.4% to 98.5%. On changed questions, accuracy rises from 55.6% to 86.5% after one round and then stays near 87%. The reader therefore looks at the image more closely rather than simply accepting more requirements. Building the reading data from the diagnosis brings no measurable benefit, however. A first-round reader trained on questions built from the fixed distribution instead answers 86.3% of the changed questions on the held-out edits of RSI, against 86.5% for our reader, so the two do equally well. Reading the model’s own generations. Program renders cannot show whether the reader also reads the model’s own generations, which are the input of every diagnosis. A blind human audit of 392 questions on these generations answers this question (Appendix D ). Accuracy rises only from 78.5% for U 0 U_{0} to 82.4% for U 3 U_{3} (Table 2 ), and every reader still accepts about a third of the requirements that humans mark as not shown. The external judge agrees, since the updated readers match it on 83% to 84% of questions, no more than U 0 U_{0} does. The reader ranks weaknesses well, however. Across pairs of chart type and question group, the Spearman correlation between the violation rates measured by the reader and by humans is 0.82 for U 0 U_{0} and 0.86 to 0.91 for later readers. The allocation rules depend on this ranking rather than on exact rates, so the diagnosis points the data to the right places even though many real errors in the model’s own images still go unreported by the reader. Structure under unseen wording. On the diagnostic set, whose wording matches training, structure accuracy rises from 82.5% to 90.3%. On BasicChartBench, whose wording never appears in training, it first drops and then recovers only partly, reaching 86.1% after round 4. Chart type and panel count still drift. The external judge sees structure recover fully, so part of this drop may come from U 0 U_{0} . Forgetting when the vocabulary changes. Round 3 replaced the old vocabulary entirely, and exact category text on the old vocabulary fell from 72% to 60% on the diagnostic set.
